work.title: Selected work
work.lede: Two case studies from start to finish, and the tools I've built along the way.

features.title: How many CI containers a test suite needs
features.text: End-to-end tests ran in 7 CI containers, one per product module. My first model balanced them and was 42% faster in a one-worker test run, but only about 8% with the 5 workers production used. Modelling the workers showed that 4 containers would be faster than 7 and cost 41% less.

link.label: Read the case study
link.sr: about how many CI containers a test suite needs

features.visualAlt: Spin Trainer's Explorer: a 13 by 13 grid of poker hands coloured by action, with range statistics
features.title: Testing a full-stack app I built for myself
features.text: A poker range trainer I use to study, and the place where I test the way I'd like to test at work. A black-box suite runs against the deployable image, the same E2E specs run against a mock and the real API, and mutation testing checks the unit tests. The suite found 8 real defects.

items.title: CI Shard Advisor
items.visualAlt: CI Shard Advisor showing a 3-container setup and the suggested moves
items.text: The pipeline idea as a public tool. It reads Cypress run reports and recommends how to split the test files across containers. I test its core with property-based, metamorphic and invariant tests.

items.title: Screen Recorder (QA mode)
items.visualAlt: The QA Bug Bench, a page with buttons that trigger console errors and failing requests
items.text: A Chrome extension for bug reports. It records console logs, network requests and each step with a ready-to-paste selector. I test it against a bug bench I built, a page that breaks on demand.

items.title: QA Wiki
items.visualAlt: The QA Wiki home page with sections on fundamentals, strategy and API testing
items.text: More than 50 articles on test strategy, API testing, Playwright, CI/CD for QA, performance testing and QA for telecom OSS/BSS. I keep adding to it.

method.title: How I work
method.quote: There's a saying in software that perfect is the enemy of good. It always grated on me a little. In maths, where I started, a proof is either right or wrong, and I think that's partly why I ended up in QA.

steps.title: Read the requirement before the code
steps.text: I join refinement and design reviews and ask what has to be true for a feature to be done. A gap found in a ticket costs a comment. Found in production, it costs a hotfix.

steps.title: State the problem precisely
steps.text: Before I test or optimize anything, I write down what is given, the rules and the goal, the way you'd state a maths problem. That's how a slow CI pipeline became a model.

link.label: See it in the CI case →

steps.title: Design tests with a named technique
steps.text: Equivalence partitioning, boundary values, decision tables, state transitions. Each test says which one it uses, so a reviewer can see what is covered and what isn't.

steps.title: Automate at the level that can fail
steps.text: Business rules and contracts get API tests with REST Assured or Karate. The flows a user sees get Playwright or Cypress. Running the same specs against a mock and the real API catches what each misses alone.

steps.title: Let the pipeline decide
steps.text: Checks run on every push and block a release when they fail. Then I keep the pipeline fast enough that nobody is tempted to skip it.

steps.title: Keep a bug open until I know why
steps.text: When something breaks, I dig until I understand the cause, and the report carries the evidence a developer needs to reproduce it. I built a Chrome extension to capture it.

Reviewed pull requests and mentored teammates on test automation.
